hints: Think about what holds the two nitrogen atoms together in $\text{N}_2$ and how much energy would be needed to break that bond to start a reaction.
Consider whether the $\text{N}\equiv\text{N}$ bond is polar or non-polar, and what that means for attack by other reagents.
walkthrough:
Picture what must break for reaction to happen**
Imagine two nitrogen atoms locked together with three shared pairs of electrons, $\text{N}\equiv\text{N}$. For nitrogen to react, that very strong linkage has to be broken first. That needs a huge input of energy, so at room temperature most collisions do not have enough energy to get started.

Check for any weak point from polarity**
Both atoms are identical, so the electrons are shared completely equally. With no $\delta+$ or $\delta-$ end, there is no site for a nucleophile or electrophile to be attracted to. Strong bond plus no polarity makes $\text{N}_2$ famously unreactive.

Final answer: $\text{N}_2$ contains a very strong triple covalent bond which requires a large amount of energy to break.
$\text{N}_2$ is non-polar so there is no partial charge for reagents to attack.

hints: Recall that a triple bond is not three identical bonds, but is made of one of one type and two of another type.
Remember the rule that the first bond formed between any two atoms is always the sigma type.
Visualise head-on overlap along the bond axis versus parallel p orbitals overlapping above and below the axis.
Count how many sigma and how many pi components that leaves in $\text{N}\equiv\text{N}$.
walkthrough:
Split the triple bond into its parts**
Think of $\text{N}\equiv\text{N}$ as $1 + 2$. The very first bond between the atoms is always a $\sigma$ bond. The second and third bonds can only form as $\pi$ bonds. So you get 1 $\sigma$ and 2 $\pi$.

See the sigma overlap head-on**
For the $\sigma$ bond, picture two orbitals pointing straight at each other along the line joining the nuclei. They meet head-on with direct overlap, giving strong electron density right between the nuclei.

See the pi overlap sideways**
For each $\pi$ bond, picture two p orbitals sitting parallel side by side, at right angles to the bond axis. They overlap sideways, giving electron density above and below the axis, not on the axis. Two such sideways overlaps give the two $\pi$ bonds.

Final answer: number of $\sigma$ bonds in $\text{N}_2$ = 1; number of $\pi$ bonds in $\text{N}_2$ = 2.
$\sigma$ bond: direct / head-on overlap of orbitals along the internuclear axis.
$\pi$ bond: sideways overlap of adjacent p orbitals above and below the axis.

hints: Write the product formula for aluminium reacting with excess chlorine and think about the usual charge on aluminium in its compounds.
walkthrough:
Use the product to read the oxidation number**
Aluminium with excess $\text{Cl}_2$ gives $\text{AlCl}_3$: $$2\text{Al} + 3\text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{AlCl}_3$$ Chlorine is more electronegative, so each Cl is -I. Three Cl give -3 total, so Al must be +III to balance to a neutral compound.

hints: Think about which electrons an atom can lose or share when it forms its highest oxide, from Na with one outer electron to Cl with seven.
walkthrough:
Link group number to highest oxide**
In the highest Period 3 oxides, every outer s and p electron is used in bonding or lost. Sodium uses 1 to give +I in $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$, magnesium uses 2 to give +II in $\text{MgO}$, right up to chlorine using 7 to give +VII. So the ceiling is set simply by how many valence electrons the atom has.
Final answer: The number of outer / valence electrons.

hints: Recall which Period 3 oxides are gases at room temperature and which are high melting point solids.
walkthrough:
Place the oxides across Period 3**
Only the oxides toward the top right like $\text{SO}_2$ and the chlorides are gases. $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ is a giant ionic lattice with a very high melting point, and $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ is a molecular solid. Both are clearly solids at room temperature.
Final answer: $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ is solid and $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ is solid at room temperature.

hints: Classify each oxide: $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ is amphoteric so it dissolves in excess strong alkali to give an aluminate, while $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ is strongly acidic.
Remember that with excess $\text{NaOH}$, the acidic oxide is fully neutralised to the phosphate salt $\text{Na}_3\text{PO}_4$ plus water, so balance Na, P, O and H.
walkthrough:
Write the amphoteric reaction for aluminium oxide**
$\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ acts as an acid with a base. With excess $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ it forms sodium tetrahydroxoaluminate: $$\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 2\text{NaOH} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{NaAl(OH)}_4$$ Check atoms: 2 Al, 2 Na, 8 O, 8 H on each side.

Write the full neutralisation for phosphorus(V) oxide**
$\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ is acidic and with excess alkali gives the normal phosphate, not the hydrogen phosphate: $$\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10} + 12\text{NaOH} \rightarrow 4\text{Na}_3\text{PO}_4 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Check atoms: 4 P, 12 Na, 22 O, 12 H on each side.

hints: Set the sum of oxidation numbers in neutral $\text{CaSiO}_3$ to zero, using +II for Ca and -II for each O.
walkthrough:
Solve with the zero sum rule**
Let Si be x. In $\text{CaSiO}_3$: $$(+2) + x + 3(-2) = 0$$ So $x - 4 = 0$, giving $x = +4$. Silicon is +IV, the same as in $\text{SiO}_2$, which makes sense as no redox occurs in this addition.

hints: Think about what happens when $\text{CaCO}_3$ is heated strongly on its own and what two products form.
walkthrough:
Recognise heating a single reactant**
Making $\text{CaO}$ from $\text{CaCO}_3$ needs only heat: $$\text{CaCO}_3 \rightarrow \text{CaO} + \text{CO}_2$$ One compound breaking down on heating into two products is the classic definition of thermal decomposition.
